card.hook: Picture a stone wall at sunset with a crowd of phones held up like tiny lanterns. That's Oia Castle, and you want to be in the front row of it.
card.stand_here: Head for Agios Nikolaos Castle (often called Oia Castle), the ruined walls and lookout terrace at the northern tip of the village. Face the village, so the cliff-top houses and two windmills sit in front of you with the sea and sunset behind them. The castle is a separate spot from the stand-here point on the map, so use the map to find your way to the northern tip.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full postcard of houses, windmills and caldera. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the windmills or one cluster of houses. Use 0.5x in the narrow lanes and for the blue domes.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest houses, then drag the slider a little darker so the whitewash keeps its detail and the sunset colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Arrive 1.5 to 2 hours before sunset, because the wall fills up early in summer. Sunset times and crowds change with the season, so check locally.
card.selfie_here: Try the Oia steps going down toward Ammoudi Bay, just below the castle walls. One travel blog says it's quieter than the top and you can often find room to frame yourself. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the village sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For the blue domes, ask someone to stand on the path just before Patisserie Medevio while you pose on the staircase down to the church (this spot is based on a blog description, so check it when you arrive).
card.rules_and_safety: The castle lookout is free to reach on foot, but check the official site before you go in case any timed-entry or access rules apply. A blog warns that the hillside "secret viewpoint" below the castle ruins is very slippery and steep, with thorny bushes, so skip it unless you climb well and wear proper shoes.
card.challenge: Keep the windmills off-centre and let the row of white houses lead the eye along the cliff, then see if you can keep the horizon dead level while 200 other people jostle for the same view.
card.good_to_know: Oia was rich in the late 19th century. In 1890 it had about 2,500 residents and around 130 sailing ships trading across the Eastern Mediterranean. The earthquake of 9 July 1956 badly damaged it, and it was rebuilt as the tourist village you see today. The 2021 census counted 1,087 people.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Agios Nikolaos Castle (often called Oia Castle), the ruined walls and lookout terrace at the northern tip of the village. Face the village, so the cliff-top houses and two windmills sit in front of you with the sea and sunset behind them. The castle is a separate spot from the stand-here point on the map, so use the map to find your way to the northern tip.

card.hook: Walk into Fira and you'll quickly find the town is too crowded and too close to see all at once. Step outside it and the whole stack of white houses finally fits in your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at Volkan on the Rocks, on the caldera path just north-west of Fira on the way toward Firostefani, just before the restaurant. Turn back to face Fira, which lies to the south-east. You don't need to go into the restaurant.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole stacked town with the caldera behind it. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched view. If your phone has higher zooms (2x to 5x), use them to pick out rooftops and church domes on the cliff.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the cliff edge on a lower line, and keep a bit of path or wall in the foreground for depth. Then tap the white walls and slide the picture a little darker so they keep their detail.
card.best_time: The rim path can get crowded at sunset. Go earlier in the evening or in the morning and you'll have more room to stand and frame your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to the promenade at the Fira cable car station, to the point where the walkway juts out. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit out so the town sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the rim path just north of town, in Firostefani, and shoot back south toward Fira's white buildings while you pose in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing people directly, and ask politely before shooting hotel rooftops or terraces, as they're private. Stay on the open path and watch your footing near the edge. The path is unlit after dark, so use your phone's flashlight on the way back.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a cruise ship in the water below, so everyone can see just how small the ship is next to the caldera.
card.good_to_know: Fira's name comes from a local way of saying "Thira", the island's ancient name. The caldera is a huge flooded volcanic crater, about 18 km from end to end on a clear day. Cruise ships often anchor between Nea Kameni and the town, which gives a handy sense of scale.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Volkan on the Rocks, on the caldera path just north-west of Fira on the way toward Firostefani, just before the restaurant. Turn back to face Fira, which lies to the south-east. You don't need to go into the restaurant.

card.hook: Most beaches give you yellow sand. Perissa gives you black sand, deep blue sea and a huge rocky mountain standing right behind it all, like it wants to be in your photo too.
card.stand_here: Perissa is about 13 km south-east of Fira. Once you're there, walk along the sand to the north end of the beach, close to the small whitewashed Church of the Holy Cross, and stand by the boulder. Face along the beach so the dark sand and sea sit beyond the boulder, with Mesa Vouno filling the background.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the sand, sea and mountain together. Tap 0.5x if you want the whole sweep of shoreline and Mesa Vouno in one frame. For the church and its bell tower, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the sand and slide it a little darker so the black sand keeps its detail and the sea and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early, from just before sunrise until about 10 AM, when the light is gentler and there are fewer people about. Just before sunrise the black sand takes on a silvery look, which is a lovely change from its usual dark self.
card.selfie_here: Climb up on the boulder at the north end of the beach, near the Mesa Vouno end where the Church of the Holy Cross stands. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the dark sand and sea in the frame. Mesa Vouno makes a dramatic backdrop behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the central square in front of the Church of the Holy Cross and frame you so the blue-domed church and its tall bell tower fill the background (the exact spot isn't fixed, so check the church's position on the map first).
card.rules_and_safety: The beach is an open public space. If you use a beach bar's loungers you may be expected to pay, so check on the spot before you sit down.
card.challenge: Take one photo where the horizon sits dead level on a gridline and the boulder is tucked into a corner, then see if anyone can guess it's sand and not charcoal.
card.good_to_know: Perissa is a village on Santorini's south-east coast, with 725 permanent residents at the 2021 census. It belongs to the community of Emporio. The remains of an Early Christian church of Saint Irene lie here, and a shortened form of her name gave the island the name Santorini.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Perissa is about 13 km south-east of Fira. Once you're there, walk along the sand to the north end of the beach, close to the small whitewashed Church of the Holy Cross, and stand by the boulder. Face along the beach so the dark sand and sea sit beyond the boulder, with Mesa Vouno filling the background.

card.hook: Picture a big black rock pushing out into the sea, a tiny white church tucked behind it, and a fishing boat chugging past at sunrise. That's the quiet corner of Kamari most people walk right by.
card.stand_here: Stand at Agios Nikolaos, on the beach beside the church at the southernmost point of Kamari Beach. Face the sea so the black rock runs out in front of you with the church behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the rock, church and sea all in one shot. Tap 0.5x to squeeze in the cliff of Mesa Vouno too. When a fishing boat passes, try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick it out.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the rock on a lower third, then tap the rock and slide a little darker so the sunrise sky and sea keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the sun comes up over the sea and the fishing boats pass. Kamari faces east, so this is a sunrise beach, not a sunset one. Late in the day the low sun warms the black pebbles and turns the cliff amber.
card.selfie_here: Head to the sand at the south end of Kamari Beach, where Mesa Vouno rises right behind you, and guides rate this corner as the beach's strongest backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the mountain fills the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on or by the stone arch at the south end and shoot north along the beach, while you stand on the sand in front so the taverna awnings and open sea fill the view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The black pebbles heat up fast and get very hot by mid-afternoon in July and August, so wear sandals or water shoes. The church is a place of worship, so be respectful and check locally before going inside.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo and wait for a fishing boat to slide past the rock, then pick your favourite moment afterwards. Bonus points if the boat lands right beside the church.
card.good_to_know: Kamari has the longest beach on Santorini, a strip of black pebbles at the foot of Mesa Vouno, which rises to about 400 m and is the island's second highest peak. The village was built by people from nearby Episkopi Gonias after the 1956 earthquake. Its name comes from a small arch (kamara) at the south end of the beach, left over from an old customs house built between 1537 and 1650.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Agios Nikolaos, on the beach beside the church at the southernmost point of Kamari Beach. Face the sea so the black rock runs out in front of you with the church behind it.

card.hook: Imerovigli is a village of about 469 people perched on the caldera rim, and its white walls will show you straight away if your phone is crooked. Good news: the gridlines fix that.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 500 m east of the subject, and face west toward the village. From there, walk west to reach the village paths for close-ups.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main view, then try 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of village and sky. For church domes and small details, go to 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon and white walls straight, then tap a white wall and slide it a little darker so the whitewash keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset is lovely, because you're facing west and the low light turns the walls warm. Early morning is usually calmer on the paths.
card.selfie_here: Try the ledge on the path above Anastasi Church, near Cilon Suites Hotel. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the blue-domed church, the pink bougainvillea and the caldera over your shoulder. Prefer whitewashed houses to a church? The stairway near Nefeli Homes has them behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street above Anastasi Church and shoot down, while you stand in front of the church gates with the blue dome and bell tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Sun protection matters from April through October: there's almost no shade on the cliff paths, and the white walls bounce the light back at you. Churches and the monastery may have their own visiting rules, so check the official site, and step aside for residents on the narrow lanes.
card.challenge: Find a church dome against a white wall and get it perfectly straight on the gridlines, with no wonky tilt allowed.
card.good_to_know: Imerovigli sits just north of Fira, with the church of Ai-Stratis at its centre. The Monastery of Saint Nikolaos is on the path between Imerovigli and Fira. On nearby Skaros Rock are the remains of a Venetian castle built in 1207 by Marco Sanudo, then ruler of all the Cyclades.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 500 m east of the subject, and face west toward the village. From there, walk west to reach the village paths for close-ups.

card.hook: Picture white houses stacked up a hill like a wedding cake, with the Aegean sitting quietly behind the rooftops. Pyrgos gives you that view for sunset, and a guide calls it quieter than the crowded spots in Oia.
card.stand_here: Head for Franco's Cafè, in the hilltop square beside the village church, and go up to its rooftop. The village centre is about 100 m to the south-west, a short walk. Face out over the Pyrgos rooftops toward the caldera and the Aegean.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the rooftops, the caldera and the sea in one shot. Tap zoom 0.5x if you want more of the square and the church in the frame. Try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single rooftop or the line of the sea.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, then tap the sky or the sea and slide it a little darker so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunset is the one to aim for. Keep the rooftops as a band in the foreground and let the sea glow behind them.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the steps just before the top of the castle ruins, right next to the entrance of Franco's Cafe. Reach them through the archway signed for Franco's. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and tilt up a bit so the ruins can fill the frame over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The rooftop is part of a bar, so expect to buy a drink. Take care if you climb around the castle ruins, because a travel blog says the walls and roofs are unstable.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the rooftops fill the bottom third and the sea fills the top, then see if you can spot a single rooftop worth zooming in on.
card.good_to_know: Pyrgos Kallistis has about 1,078 people (2021 census) and is built in tiers up a hill. At the top are the ruins of a Venetian castle, Kasteli, which was once the island's administrative centre. The old part has narrow, winding lanes, fortified walls and hidden passages, and it's described as one of the least spoiled by tourism on Santorini.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Franco's Cafè, in the hilltop square beside the village church, and go up to its rooftop. The village centre is about 100 m to the south-west, a short walk. Face out over the Pyrgos rooftops toward the caldera and the Aegean.

card.hook: Picture a rusty-red cliff dropping onto dark sand, with bright blue sea along the bottom. It looks like someone planned the colours. The best view of it is from above, and you don't have to go down to get it.
card.stand_here: Head for the clifftop viewpoint at the trail head above Red Beach, about 230 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and you'll be looking down on the red cliff wall and the dark beach. Stay well back from the edge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole cliff and the beach below. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural view. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the colour and texture of the cliff face.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red cliff, then slide it a little darker so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: One guide recommends 14:00-16:00, when the sun is on the cliff and the red looks strongest. Early morning and late afternoon are also suggested, and they're quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Try the eastern end of Red Beach, where the cliffs rise from the sea, or beside the big boulder at the water's edge. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the red cliffs and turquoise sea behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a fellow visitor at the clifftop viewpoint on the trail above the beach to take your photo, with the beach and red cliffs in frame below you, and keep well back from the edge yourself.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the beach have been out of bounds since 2013 and the path down is often closed because of rockfall, so check the current situation before you set out. Signs warn of falling rocks, so keep clear of the cliff base when posing, and never lean out over the edge for a better angle.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the lower third line, and see if you can get the red cliff to fill the frame without your shadow sneaking in.
card.good_to_know: Red Beach is a volcanic sand beach near the village of Akrotiri. The red tint comes from oxidised iron, and the sand is a mix of red and black crushed volcanic rock from the nearby caldera. For a second photo, the lighthouse at Akrotiri is a good sunset alternative, with Red Beach visible in the distance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the clifftop viewpoint at the trail head above Red Beach, about 230 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and you'll be looking down on the red cliff wall and the dark beach. Stay well back from the edge.

card.hook: You've just trotted down a very long flight of steps, and your legs have earned this: painted wooden boats bobbing in the water, tavernas lining the edge and red cliffs with Oia piled up behind.
card.stand_here: Stand at the widest part of the waterfront path among the tavernas, then turn to look south, down toward the bay. The boats sit in front of you and the red cliffs and Oia rise behind.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to squeeze boats, cliffs and Oia into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a single boat or the cliff-top houses.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the boats, slide the brightness a touch darker so the sky and bright cliffs keep their colour, and use the gridlines to line the waterline up with one of them.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, around the golden hours, when it's calmer than the sunset rush. Sunset is a popular time to be here, so expect company if you stay for it.
card.selfie_here: For a quieter selfie, stand on the Oia steps a little above the bottom, just below Oia Castle, and frame yourself with the bay over your shoulder. At water level, the rocky platform by the boats works too, with the cliffs rising behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep your arm low so the cliffs fit in.
card.ask_someone: Walk through the tavernas to the widest stretch of the path and ask a passer-by to photograph you with the harbour boats and red cliffs behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: There are no lifeguards at Ammoudi Bay, and getting into the water means slippery volcanic rock or a jump into deep water, so it's not for very young children or non-swimmers. Take your time on the steps and carry water if it's warm.
card.challenge: Find the most colourful boat in the harbour and get it in the foreground with the cliffs filling the frame behind it.
card.good_to_know: Ammoudi Bay is the little harbour at the foot of the cliffs below Oia, and the buildings at the base of the cliffs belong to the village of Ormos Armeni. Many sailing tours start here, so there's usually something happening on the water. Guides disagree on the number of steps (around 200, or maybe 250-300), and you have to climb them back up afterwards.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the widest part of the waterfront path among the tavernas, then turn to look south, down toward the bay. The boats sit in front of you and the red cliffs and Oia rise behind.

selfie_research.safety: There are no lifeguards at Ammoudi Bay, and entry is from slippery volcanic rock or a jump into deep water; the guide says it is not suitable for very young children or non-swimmers.
selfie_research.notes: Sources disagree on the number of steps down to the bay (about 200, 214, 290 and 300+), so allow for a tiring walk back up. The castle-wall spot on Oia Castle faces the bay, so I did not list it as a selfie spot because the bay would be in front of you, not behind. The rocky-platform tip comes from a generic beach guide with no named location. The steps spot is an inferred selfie use of a blog's suggestion to frame yourself, not an explicit selfie recommendation. Map positions were not checked against the given coordinates.

card.hook: Here's the funny thing about the Three Bells: walk right up to the church and you'll struggle to get the whole thing in. The forecourt is too close to fit the blue dome, the bells and the sea into one frame, so step back and let the caldera do the work.
card.stand_here: Head for Santorini Palace Hotel and stand in the parking area further west toward the sea, not the church forecourt. The church lies to the west of you, so face it with the dome and bell tower sitting against the open caldera.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the dome, bells and caldera together. Then try 2x to bring the sea in closer behind the bells. Save 0.5x for the cliff path, and keep your phone level because it stretches the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white wall, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky stays blue and the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Try to avoid sunset and cruise-ship hours, because the area gets crowded then. One guide says the small ledge and lower walkway are quieter after 5pm, but check the light on the day.
card.selfie_here: Walk around the back of the church, follow the signs marked 'Viewpoint', and use the low wall there. It's a handy place to sit, and it tends to be less crowded than the front. Use your front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it on the front) and keep the blue dome and bells over your shoulder. You can also try the small ledge and lower walkway near the church, where there's room to try a few poses.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the parking lot west of Santorini Palace Hotel, toward the sea, because that's where the church is framed like the postcards.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is still in use, so be quiet and respectful, and cover your shoulders and knees. Check the official site for any visiting rules. The cliff paths can be slippery and one visitor says people have fallen, so wear suitable footwear.
card.challenge: Take your photo from two different spots, like the parking area and the back viewpoint, then pick a winner. Everyone has a favourite side.
card.good_to_know: This is officially the Catholic Church of the Dormition, and the present building dates from 1757. It was restored after the 1956 Amorgos earthquake. Two small cave churches were cut into the cliff in the mid-17th century, but they were lost as the cliff face wore away. The feast day is 15 August.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Santorini Palace Hotel and stand in the parking area further west toward the sea, not the church forecourt. The church lies to the west of you, so face it with the dome and bell tower sitting against the open caldera.

selfie_spots.why: Sources say this rear vantage point gives the classic postcard framing of the blue dome and bells against the sea, and it tends to be less crowded than the front.

selfie_research.notes: No page states any rule about selfie sticks or tripods. One guide only advises that a tripod can help for sunset shots but should be used mindfully given crowds; I treated that as advice, not a rule, and did not list it. Sources disagree on the area: several place the church in Firostefani, others in Fira, and the coordinates you gave fit the church area. One page names the church 'Agios Theodoros', which conflicts with the official name 'Catholic Church of the Dormition' given by others. The Santorini Palace Hotel parking-lot tip comes from a single reviewer, and the car park above the church (Phil and Garth, Onceuponajrny) is a second option for a passer-by shot. Some pages are 1–3 years old, so check access and the parking lot before visiting. The selfie-spot descriptions are my paraphrase of the sources, which describe the photo positions only loosely; confirm the exact wall or ledge on arrival.
